# Diagnosing Heating System Behavior in Stationary vs. Driven Conditions

A car's heating system functions as a thermal management subsystem, relying on fluid dynamics that are fundamentally different from those governing propulsion. When you observe heat output only after driving for a minute, the root cause is almost certainly coolant flow rather than a lack of electric power or actuator failure. The heater core is essentially a secondary radiator located inside your HVAC unit; it requires a continuous stream of hot coolant to transfer thermal energy into the cabin air.

Your specific symptomâno heat when stationary at 2Â°C, with heat appearing only after drivingâpoints directly to a circulation bottleneck. When the vehicle is idling, the water pump operates at its lowest duty cycle. In many modern engine architectures, this low-RPM flow might be insufficient to push coolant through a restricted passage. Once you engage the drivetrain and rev the engine, the increased RPM of the crankshaft drives the water pump faster, increasing flow velocity enough to overcome the restriction. This explains why the slight heat detected during idle was likely just the beginning of the thermal cycle, and why moving off resolved the issue immediately.

Given your history of an overheated engine due to a radiator leak and subsequent replacement of the engine, radiator, and thermostat, the diagnostic focus must be on the integrity of the cooling loop. A common failure mode in this scenario is a partially clogged heater core or a compromised hose connection. If debris from old sludge lodged in the system during your repair, it could have settled in the narrow inlet to the heater core. At idle flow rates, this debris acts as a choke point, starving the core of hot fluid. Higher flow rates bypass this restriction more effectively, restoring heat transfer.

Another critical component to evaluate is the thermostat itself. Although you replaced it, verify that it opens fully at its rated temperature (typically 82Â°C to 90Â°C for most automotive applications). If the thermostat remains partially closed during warm-up, the coolant may not reach the operating temperature required to provide cabin heat, regardless of flow rate. However, your observation that the system works fine after driving suggests the engine reaches peak temperature; thus, the issue is likely flow dynamics rather than temperature regulation.

To isolate the fault without disassembly, you can perform a simple pressure test on the cooling system with the engine cold. A drop in pressure indicates an external leak, but a lack of pressure retention could also suggest an internal blockage or a failing head gasket allowing combustion gases into the coolant passages. If the system holds pressure but flow is restricted, inspect the upper and lower radiator hoses for soft spots or collapses that might pinch off flow at low speeds. Additionally, check the heater control valve (common in some European models). A stuck-closed valve will prevent coolant from entering the heater core entirely until thermal expansion or vibration forces it open, which often happens after driving.

If you are comfortable with diagnostics, a block test using an infrared thermometer on the inlet and outlet hoses of the heater core can reveal flow issues. If the inlet hose is hot but the outlet is cool while the engine is idling, the core is restricted. Once the car is driven and flow increases, the temperature differential should decrease significantly.

While your recent repairs likely resolved the overheating crisis, the heating anomaly suggests the cooling system has not fully purged all contaminants or that a specific restriction remains. Addressing this now prevents future issues where low-idle performance (such as in traffic or parking) could lead to localized boiling points and potential engine damage.
